name: General Reasoning Knowledge
description: Broad concepts Chiedza can reason with. Each concept has a plain definition, how it works, why it matters, an example and related ideas. Edit or add concepts to teach the AI more.

concepts.title: Photosynthesis
concepts.summary: The process plants use to turn sunlight, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen.
concepts.definition: Photosynthesis is how green plants, algae and some bacteria make their own food. They use light energy to combine water and carbon dioxide into glucose (a sugar) and release oxygen.
how: Roots take in water and leaves take in carbon dioxide through tiny pores called stomata.
Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts absorbs sunlight and uses that energy to split water.
Hydrogen from the water joins carbon dioxide to make glucose, and oxygen is released as a by-product.
concepts.why: It is the base of almost every food chain and it produces the oxygen animals breathe.
concepts.example: A maize plant in a sunny field uses water from the soil and carbon dioxide from the air to grow cobs, while giving off oxygen.

concepts.title: The water cycle
concepts.summary: Water moves between the ground, the air and the sea in a continuous loop.
concepts.definition: The water cycle is the journey water takes as it evaporates from oceans, lakes and soil, condenses into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and flows back to the sea.
how: The sun heats water, which evaporates into invisible water vapour.
As the vapour rises it cools and condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds.
Droplets join until they are heavy enough to fall as precipitation (rain, hail or snow).
Water runs over land or soaks into the ground and eventually returns to rivers and oceans.
concepts.why: It supplies fresh water for drinking, farming and life, and it moves heat around the planet.
concepts.example: Water from Lake Kariba evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain on Harare, and flows back down rivers to the lake.

concepts.title: Gravity
concepts.summary: The force that pulls objects with mass toward each other.
concepts.definition: Gravity is a force of attraction between any two objects that have mass. The more mass an object has, the stronger its pull, and the pull weakens with distance.
how: Every object with mass attracts every other object.
On Earth the pull is strong enough to keep us on the ground and to make dropped things fall.
Gravity also keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and the planets orbiting the Sun.
concepts.why: Gravity shapes the universe, gives us weight, and makes tides, orbits and falling motion possible.
concepts.example: A ball thrown into the air always curves back down because Earth's gravity pulls it toward the centre of the planet.

concepts.title: Electricity
concepts.summary: The flow of electric charge, usually electrons moving through a conductor.
concepts.definition: Electricity is the movement of electric charge. In a wire, electrons flow when a voltage pushes them, and this current can carry energy to lights, motors and devices.
how: A source such as a battery or generator creates a voltage difference.
The voltage pushes electrons through a closed circuit.
The moving electrons transfer energy to components like bulbs, which convert it into light and heat.
concepts.why: Electricity powers homes, schools, hospitals, phones and almost all modern technology.
concepts.example: Closing a switch completes a circuit so electrons flow from a battery through a bulb and back, making it glow.

concepts.title: Magnetism
concepts.summary: A force that attracts or repels certain materials, caused by moving electric charge.
concepts.definition: Magnetism is a force produced by moving electric charges. Magnets have a north and a south pole; like poles repel and opposite poles attract.
how: Inside a magnet, groups of atoms line up so their tiny magnetic fields add together.
This creates a magnetic field around the magnet.
The field pulls on magnetic materials such as iron and on other magnets.
concepts.why: Magnetism is used in motors, generators, speakers, hard drives and compasses.
concepts.example: A compass needle turns to line up with Earth's magnetic field, pointing roughly north.

concepts.title: Light
concepts.summary: A form of energy that travels in waves and lets us see.
concepts.definition: Light is electromagnetic radiation that our eyes can detect. It travels in straight lines, can reflect off surfaces and bend (refract) when it passes between materials.
how: Light travels from a source in straight lines at about 300,000 km per second.
When it hits an object it can be absorbed, reflected or scattered.
When it passes from air into water or glass it bends, which is why a straw looks broken in a glass.
concepts.why: Light lets us see, drives photosynthesis, and carries information through fibre-optic cables.
concepts.example: White light splits into a rainbow when it refracts through water droplets because each colour bends by a different amount.

concepts.title: Sound
concepts.summary: Vibrations that travel through a material as waves and are heard by the ear.
concepts.definition: Sound is a pressure wave created by vibrating objects. It needs a medium such as air, water or a solid to travel through and cannot travel through a vacuum.
how: An object vibrates and pushes nearby air molecules together and apart.
The wave of pressure travels outward.
The ear collects the wave and the brain interprets it as sound.
concepts.why: Sound lets us communicate, enjoy music and detect danger.
concepts.example: A drum skin vibrates when struck, sending pressure waves through the air to your ears.

concepts.title: Energy
concepts.summary: The ability to do work or cause change; it cannot be created or destroyed, only changed in form.
concepts.definition: Energy is the capacity to do work. It comes in forms such as kinetic (movement), potential (stored), thermal, chemical, electrical and light energy.
how: Energy changes from one form to another but the total amount stays the same.
For example, chemical energy in food becomes kinetic energy when you run.
Renewable sources like sunlight, wind and water are continually replenished.
concepts.why: Everything that happens — growth, movement, heating, thinking — involves energy transfer.
concepts.example: A falling ball changes potential energy into kinetic energy, and some becomes heat and sound on impact.

concepts.title: Force and motion
concepts.summary: A push or pull that can change an object's speed, direction or shape.
concepts.definition: A force is a push or pull acting on an object. Unbalanced forces change motion; balanced forces keep an object still or moving steadily.
how: Forces act on objects in particular directions.
When forces are unbalanced, the object speeds up, slows down or changes direction.
Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces.
concepts.why: Forces explain how everything moves, from bicycles to rockets.
concepts.example: A ball rolls farther on smooth ground than on rough ground because there is less friction.

concepts.title: Atoms and matter
concepts.summary: Atoms are the tiny building blocks that make up all matter.
concepts.definition: An atom is the smallest unit of an element. It has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. Atoms join to form molecules.
how: Protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus at the centre.
Electrons move around the nucleus in shells.
Atoms bond together by sharing or transferring electrons to form compounds.
concepts.why: Understanding atoms explains chemistry, materials, medicines and life itself.
concepts.example: Two hydrogen atoms bond with one oxygen atom to make a water molecule (H2O).

concepts.title: The solar system
concepts.summary: The Sun and everything that orbits it, including eight planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
concepts.definition: The solar system is the Sun and all the objects bound to it by gravity. The eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
how: The Sun holds most of the mass and its gravity keeps the planets in orbit.
Planets orbit at different distances and speeds.
Moons orbit planets, while asteroids and comets follow their own paths.
concepts.why: It is our home in space and helps us understand seasons, tides and the possibility of life elsewhere.
concepts.example: Earth takes about 365 days to orbit the Sun once, which gives us our year.

concepts.title: Seasons
concepts.summary: Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted as it orbits the Sun.
concepts.definition: Seasons are caused by the 23.5-degree tilt of Earth's axis. Different parts of Earth receive sunlight at different angles through the year.
how: Earth orbits the Sun while spinning on a tilted axis.
When your hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight is more direct and days are longer (summer).
When it tilts away, sunlight is slanted and days are shorter (winter).
concepts.why: Seasons control weather, farming cycles and daylight hours.
concepts.example: Zimbabwe has a warm, rainy season and a cooler, dry season because of the tilt and its position in the southern hemisphere.

concepts.title: Earthquakes
concepts.summary: Sudden shaking of the ground caused by movement of rock along faults.
concepts.definition: An earthquake is the shaking that happens when energy stored in rocks is suddenly released, usually along a fault where tectonic plates move.
how: Tectonic plates push against each other and stress builds up in the rock.
The rock suddenly slips along a fault, releasing energy.
Seismic waves spread out from the focus and shake the ground.
concepts.why: Earthquakes can cause great damage and help scientists understand how the planet moves.
concepts.example: The ground shakes when a fault slips, and the strength is measured on the Richter or moment magnitude scale.

concepts.title: Volcanoes
concepts.summary: Openings in Earth's surface where magma, ash and gases escape.
concepts.definition: A volcano is a vent in the crust through which molten rock (magma), ash and gas reach the surface. Once magma reaches the surface it is called lava.
how: Magma forms deep underground where rock melts.
Pressure pushes the magma up through cracks and a central vent.
It erupts as lava, ash and gas, and cools to form new rock.
concepts.why: Volcanoes build new land, enrich soil and reveal what is inside the Earth.
concepts.example: Volcanic ash can make very fertile soil, which is why people farm near some volcanoes.

concepts.title: Erosion
concepts.summary: The wearing away and movement of rock and soil by water, wind or ice.
concepts.definition: Erosion is the process where natural forces carry away soil and rock. Weathering breaks the material down and erosion moves it.
how: Water, wind or ice loosens and breaks up rock and soil.
The material is carried downhill or downwind.
It is deposited somewhere else, often in rivers, valleys or the sea.
concepts.why: Erosion shapes landscapes but can destroy farmland and cause landslides.
concepts.example: Heavy rain on bare soil washes the topsoil into rivers, leaving the field less fertile.

concepts.title: Ecosystems
concepts.summary: A community of living things interacting with each other and their environment.
concepts.definition: An ecosystem is made of living organisms (plants, animals, microbes) and the non-living parts of their environment (water, soil, air, sunlight) interacting together.
how: Producers such as plants capture energy from the sun.
Consumers eat producers or other consumers, forming food chains and webs.
Decomposers break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil.
concepts.why: Healthy ecosystems provide food, clean water, clean air and stability for all life.
concepts.example: A river ecosystem includes plants, fish, insects, birds and the water and soil they depend on.

concepts.title: Food chains and webs
concepts.summary: The path energy takes from plants through animals that eat them.
concepts.definition: A food chain shows who eats whom, starting with a producer. A food web is many food chains linked together.
how: Producers (plants) capture sunlight energy.
Herbivores eat the plants.
Carnivores eat the herbivores, and decomposers recycle the nutrients.
concepts.why: Food chains show how energy moves and why removing one species can affect many others.
concepts.example: Grass is eaten by a grasshopper, which is eaten by a frog, which is eaten by a snake.

concepts.title: Biodiversity
concepts.summary: The variety of living things in a place, from genes to species to ecosystems.
concepts.definition: Biodiversity is the variety of life. It includes differences within a species, between species, and between whole ecosystems.
how: Many species evolve and fill different roles in an ecosystem.
More variety makes ecosystems more resilient to change.
Habitat loss, pollution and climate change reduce biodiversity.
concepts.why: Biodiversity keeps ecosystems stable and provides food, medicine and materials.
concepts.example: A forest with many plant and animal species can recover better from disease than a single-species plantation.

concepts.title: Climate change
concepts.summary: Long-term shifts in temperature and weather caused mainly by human greenhouse-gas emissions.
concepts.definition: Climate change is the long-term change in Earth's climate, especially the warming caused by burning fossil fuels and releasing greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane.
how: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Greenhouse gases trap heat that would otherwise escape into space.
More trapped heat raises average temperatures, changing rainfall, ice and sea levels.
concepts.why: It threatens food and water supplies, causes extreme weather and endangers coastal communities.
concepts.example: Melting glaciers and more frequent droughts are signs of a warming climate.

concepts.title: The greenhouse effect
concepts.summary: The way certain gases in the atmosphere trap heat and keep Earth warm.
concepts.definition: The greenhouse effect is the warming of Earth's surface because gases in the atmosphere absorb and re-emit heat. It is natural and necessary, but human emissions strengthen it.
how: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the ground.
The ground gives off heat as infrared radiation.
Greenhouse gases absorb some of that heat and send it back, keeping Earth warm.
concepts.why: A natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable; too much of it causes global warming.
concepts.example: Without any greenhouse effect Earth would be far colder, but adding extra carbon dioxide makes it warmer than normal.

concepts.title: Pollution
concepts.summary: Harmful substances released into the environment.
concepts.definition: Pollution is the introduction of harmful materials into air, water or land. It can come from factories, vehicles, farms, litter and waste.
how: Human activities release pollutants into the environment.
Pollutants build up in air, water or soil.
They harm plants, animals and people, and can enter the food chain.
concepts.why: Pollution causes disease, damages ecosystems and contributes to climate change.
concepts.example: Plastic bags that reach rivers can be eaten by fish and end up in the food chain.

concepts.title: Recycling
concepts.summary: Turning used materials into new products instead of throwing them away.
concepts.definition: Recycling is collecting and processing used materials such as paper, glass, plastic and metal so they can be made into new products.
how: Used materials are collected and sorted.
They are cleaned and processed into raw material.
The material is used to make new products, saving energy and resources.
concepts.why: Recycling reduces landfill waste, saves energy and lowers pollution.
concepts.example: Old plastic bottles can be recycled into new bottles or clothing fibres.

concepts.title: The digestive system
concepts.summary: How the body breaks food down into nutrients it can use.
concepts.definition: Digestion is the process of breaking food into small molecules that can be absorbed into the blood. It starts in the mouth and continues through the stomach and intestines.
how: Teeth and saliva break food into smaller pieces and start digesting starch.
The stomach churns food with acid and enzymes.
The small intestine absorbs nutrients, and the large intestine absorbs water before waste leaves the body.
concepts.why: Digestion supplies the body with energy and building materials.
concepts.example: A piece of bread is chewed, broken down in the stomach and its sugars are absorbed in the small intestine.

concepts.title: Respiration
concepts.summary: The process cells use to release energy from food, using oxygen and producing carbon dioxide.
concepts.definition: Respiration is the chemical process in cells that releases energy from glucose. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water.
how: Oxygen enters the body through the lungs and is carried by blood.
Cells use oxygen to break down glucose.
Energy is released for the body to use, and carbon dioxide is carried back to the lungs and breathed out.
concepts.why: Respiration powers every cell and is the opposite of photosynthesis in terms of gases.
concepts.example: When you run, your muscles respire faster, so you breathe harder to get more oxygen.

concepts.title: The circulatory system
concepts.summary: The heart, blood and blood vessels that carry oxygen and nutrients around the body.
concepts.definition: The circulatory system moves blood through the body. The heart pumps it, arteries carry it away from the heart and veins bring it back.
how: The heart pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body through arteries.
Tiny capillaries deliver oxygen and nutrients to cells and pick up waste.
Veins carry the blood back to the heart and lungs to get more oxygen.
concepts.why: Every cell needs a constant supply of oxygen and nutrients and a way to remove waste.
concepts.example: Your heart beats faster when you exercise so more oxygen reaches your muscles.

concepts.title: The immune system
concepts.summary: The body's defence system against germs and disease.
concepts.definition: The immune system is a network of cells, tissues and organs that defend the body against bacteria, viruses and other threats.
how: Skin and mucus form barriers that keep germs out.
White blood cells detect and attack invaders.
Some cells remember the germ so the body can respond faster next time.
concepts.why: It keeps us healthy and is the basis of how vaccines work.
concepts.example: After you recover from a virus, memory cells help your body fight it quickly if it returns.

concepts.title: Vaccines
concepts.summary: A medicine that trains the immune system to fight a disease without making you sick.
concepts.definition: A vaccine contains a harmless part or weakened form of a germ. It teaches the immune system to recognise and fight that germ.
how: The vaccine introduces a harmless version of the germ.
The immune system responds and makes antibodies.
Memory cells remain, so the body can fight the real germ quickly.
concepts.why: Vaccines prevent serious illness and protect whole communities through herd immunity.
concepts.example: The measles vaccine protects a child from measles by training their immune system in advance.

concepts.title: Nutrition
concepts.summary: Getting the right nutrients the body needs to grow and stay healthy.
concepts.definition: Nutrition is about the food the body needs: carbohydrates for energy, proteins for growth and repair, fats for energy and vitamins and minerals for health.
how: Eat a variety of foods from different groups.
Include fruits and vegetables for vitamins and fibre.
Drink enough water and limit sugary and highly processed foods.
concepts.why: Good nutrition supports growth, learning, immunity and long-term health.
concepts.example: A balanced meal might include sadza (carbohydrate), beans (protein), greens (vitamins) and water.

concepts.title: Sleep
concepts.summary: A regular state of rest that the brain and body need to repair and remember.
concepts.definition: Sleep is a natural state of reduced consciousness that the body uses to repair tissues, consolidate memories and regulate hormones.
how: The brain cycles through light and deep sleep stages.
During deep sleep the body repairs itself and growth hormones are released.
REM sleep helps process emotions and memories.
concepts.why: Lack of sleep harms concentration, mood, immunity and health.
concepts.example: Students who sleep well remember what they studied better than those who stay up all night.

concepts.title: Exercise
concepts.summary: Physical activity that strengthens the body and improves health.
concepts.definition: Exercise is planned physical activity that raises heart rate and works muscles. It improves fitness, strength and mood.
how: Muscles use more oxygen and energy during activity.
The heart and lungs become stronger with regular exercise.
The body releases endorphins that improve mood.
concepts.why: Exercise protects against disease, builds strength and supports mental health.
concepts.example: Walking, running, football or dancing for 30 minutes a day improves fitness.

concepts.title: Mental health
concepts.summary: How we think, feel and cope with everyday life.
concepts.definition: Mental health is our emotional and psychological wellbeing. It affects how we handle stress, relate to others and make choices.
how: Sleep, exercise, nutrition and supportive relationships protect mental health.
Talking about feelings helps reduce stress.
When difficulties last or feel overwhelming, professional help is important.
concepts.why: Mental health affects learning, relationships and physical health.
concepts.example: Taking a break, breathing slowly and talking to a trusted person can help when you feel stressed.

concepts.title: The internet
concepts.summary: A global network of computers that send data to each other using shared rules.
concepts.definition: The internet is a worldwide network of connected computers. Data is broken into packets and sent between devices using protocols such as TCP/IP.
how: Your device sends a request to a router, which connects to your internet provider.
The request travels through cables and networks to a server.
The server sends data back in packets, which your device reassembles.
concepts.why: The internet enables communication, learning, business and access to information worldwide.
concepts.example: When you open a website, your browser asks a server for the page and displays the files it receives.

concepts.title: Computers
concepts.summary: Machines that process information using hardware and software.
concepts.definition: A computer is a machine that takes input, processes it using a central processing unit (CPU), stores data in memory and produces output.
how: Input devices such as keyboards send data into the computer.
The CPU follows instructions from software to process the data.
Results are stored in memory or shown on output devices such as screens.
concepts.why: Computers power communication, education, science, business and entertainment.
concepts.example: When you type a letter, the keyboard sends signals, the CPU processes them and the screen shows the letters.

concepts.title: Artificial intelligence
concepts.summary: Computer systems that perform tasks that normally need human intelligence.
concepts.definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that can learn patterns from data and make decisions or predictions. Machine learning is a common approach where models improve with examples.
how: Large amounts of data are collected and prepared.
A model is trained to find patterns in the data.
The trained model makes predictions or decisions on new data.
concepts.why: AI is used in medicine, transport, education and communication, but it must be used carefully and fairly.
concepts.example: A spam filter learns from many emails to recognise which new messages are likely to be spam.

concepts.title: Algorithms
concepts.summary: A clear set of steps for solving a problem or completing a task.
concepts.definition: An algorithm is a finite sequence of clear instructions that takes an input and produces an output. Computer programs are algorithms written in code.
how: Define the problem and the input.
Write clear, ordered steps to process the input.
Test the steps and improve them if the result is wrong.
concepts.why: Algorithms are the foundation of all software and help us solve problems systematically.
concepts.example: A recipe is like an algorithm: follow the steps in order and you get the dish.

concepts.title: Encryption
concepts.summary: Scrambling data so only the right person can read it.
concepts.definition: Encryption converts readable data into a coded form using a key. Only someone with the correct key can decrypt it back.
how: Plain data is combined with a key using a mathematical process.
The result looks like random characters.
The receiver uses the key to decrypt and read the data.
concepts.why: Encryption protects messages, bank details and private information online.
concepts.example: When you shop online, your card details are encrypted so others cannot read them.

concepts.title: Democracy
concepts.summary: A system where people choose their leaders and have a say in decisions.
concepts.definition: Democracy is a form of government in which power comes from the people, usually through free and fair elections and protected rights.
how: Citizens vote for representatives or decide issues directly.
Elected leaders make laws within a constitution.
Rights, courts and free media help hold leaders accountable.
concepts.why: Democracy gives people a voice and protects freedoms, though it depends on participation and strong institutions.
concepts.example: In a general election, citizens vote for the party or candidate they want to represent them.

concepts.title: A constitution
concepts.summary: The highest set of rules that defines how a country is governed.
concepts.definition: A constitution is the supreme law of a country. It sets out the structure of government, the powers of leaders and the rights of citizens.
how: It establishes institutions such as the legislature, executive and courts.
It lists citizens' rights and limits on government power.
Laws and actions must comply with it, and courts can strike down those that do not.
concepts.why: It prevents abuse of power and protects citizens' rights.
concepts.example: A court can declare a law invalid if it goes against the constitution.

concepts.title: Human rights
concepts.summary: Basic rights every person has simply because they are human.
concepts.definition: Human rights are the freedoms and protections that belong to every person, such as the right to life, education, safety, equality and free expression.
how: Rights are recognised in national constitutions and international agreements.
Laws and institutions are meant to protect them.
People and organisations speak up when rights are violated.
concepts.why: They protect dignity and fairness, especially for people who are vulnerable.
concepts.example: The right to education means every child should be able to go to school.

concepts.title: Inflation
concepts.summary: A general rise in prices over time, which means money buys less.
concepts.definition: Inflation is the rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services rises. When inflation is high, each unit of money buys fewer things.
how: Demand can grow faster than the supply of goods.
Costs such as fuel or wages can rise and be passed on as higher prices.
Too much money circulating can also push prices up.
concepts.why: Inflation affects savings, wages and the cost of living, especially for poorer households.
concepts.example: If a loaf of bread costs $1 today and $1.20 next year, that is inflation.

concepts.title: Supply and demand
concepts.summary: How prices are set by how much is available and how much people want.
concepts.definition: Supply is how much of a good is available; demand is how much people want it. Prices tend to rise when demand is high and supply is low, and fall when supply is high and demand is low.
how: Buyers compete for goods, which pushes prices up when supply is short.
Sellers compete for customers, which pushes prices down when there is plenty.
The market settles at a price where supply and demand balance.
concepts.why: It explains prices, shortages and why markets change.
concepts.example: Tomato prices rise when a drought reduces the harvest but people still want to buy them.

concepts.title: Budgeting
concepts.summary: Planning how to spend and save the money you have.
concepts.definition: A budget is a plan for income and expenses over a period. It helps you spend on needs first, save regularly and avoid debt.
how: List all your income.
List your needs and wants, and add up the costs.
Spend on needs first, set aside savings, then allow for wants within what is left.
concepts.why: Budgeting helps you avoid debt, reach goals and handle emergencies.
concepts.example: A family budget might put 50% toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings.

concepts.title: Saving
concepts.summary: Setting money aside for future needs and goals.
concepts.definition: Saving is keeping part of your income instead of spending it, so you can use it later for goals or emergencies.
how: Decide on a savings goal and a regular amount.
Move the money to a safe place before you spend it.
Review your progress and adjust when needed.
concepts.why: Savings provide security and make big goals possible.
concepts.example: Saving a small amount each week can add up to enough for school supplies or an emergency.

concepts.title: Interest
concepts.summary: The cost of borrowing money or the reward for saving it.
concepts.definition: Interest is a percentage paid for the use of money. When you save, the bank may pay you interest; when you borrow, you pay interest to the lender.
how: The interest rate is applied to the amount of money involved.
Simple interest is calculated on the original amount.
Compound interest is calculated on the original amount plus interest already earned, so it grows faster.
concepts.why: Understanding interest helps you save wisely and avoid expensive debt.
concepts.example: $100 saved at 10% simple interest earns $10 in a year.

concepts.title: Entrepreneurship
concepts.summary: Starting and running a business to solve a problem and create value.
concepts.definition: Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying an opportunity, organising resources and taking on risk to create a business.
how: Find a real problem people will pay to solve.
Plan your product, costs, customers and pricing.
Start small, test with real customers and improve.
concepts.why: Entrepreneurs create jobs, solve problems and grow economies.
concepts.example: A young person who bakes and sells cakes at school is practising entrepreneurship.

concepts.title: Marketing
concepts.summary: How a business tells people about its products and persuades them to buy.
concepts.definition: Marketing is the process of understanding customers and promoting products or services so people know about them and want them.
how: Understand who your customers are and what they need.
Decide on a clear message and a fair price.
Reach customers through channels such as word of mouth, social media or local advertising.
concepts.why: Even a great product fails if nobody knows about it.
concepts.example: A bakery markets itself by posting photos of fresh bread and offering a small discount on Mondays.

concepts.title: Nouns
concepts.summary: A noun is a word that names a person, place, thing or idea.
concepts.definition: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. Common nouns are general (dog, city) and proper nouns name specific things and start with a capital letter (Harare, Tendai).
how: Ask: who or what is this sentence about?
If the word names a person, place, thing or idea, it is a noun.
Check whether it is common (general) or proper (specific).
concepts.why: Nouns are the building blocks of sentences because they tell us what we are talking about.
concepts.example: In 'Rudo lives in Bulawayo', 'Rudo' and 'Bulawayo' are proper nouns.

concepts.title: Verbs
concepts.summary: A verb is a word that shows an action or a state of being.
concepts.definition: A verb tells us what the subject does or is. Action verbs show actions (run, write) and state verbs show being or feeling (is, seem, love).
how: Find the subject of the sentence.
Ask what the subject does or is.
The word that answers is the verb.
concepts.why: Every complete sentence needs a verb to show what is happening.
concepts.example: In 'The children sing loudly', 'sing' is the verb.

concepts.title: Metaphors and similes
concepts.summary: Ways of comparing things to create vivid meaning.
concepts.definition: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'. A metaphor says one thing is another to create a strong image.
how: Notice the two things being compared.
Check whether 'like' or 'as' is used (simile) or a direct comparison (metaphor).
Work out the quality the writer wants you to imagine.
concepts.why: Figurative language makes writing clearer, richer and more memorable.
concepts.example: 'Her smile was sunshine' is a metaphor; 'her smile was like sunshine' is a simile.

concepts.title: Critical thinking
concepts.summary: Thinking carefully about whether a claim is true and well supported.
concepts.definition: Critical thinking is the habit of questioning claims, checking evidence, spotting assumptions and considering other explanations before deciding what to believe.
how: Identify the claim and the evidence offered.
Ask whether the source is reliable and whether there is bias.
Consider alternative explanations and decide what the evidence supports.
concepts.why: It protects us from misinformation and helps us make better decisions.
concepts.example: Before sharing a shocking post, check who wrote it and whether other reliable sources agree.

concepts.title: Problem solving
concepts.summary: A structured way to find a solution to a difficulty.
concepts.definition: Problem solving is the process of understanding a problem, choosing a strategy, trying it and checking the result.
how: Understand the problem and what a good solution would look like.
Break it into smaller parts and choose a strategy.
Try it, check the result and change the plan if needed.
concepts.why: It turns overwhelming problems into manageable steps.
concepts.example: If you are behind on homework, list the tasks, do the most urgent first and ask for help where needed.

concepts.title: Teamwork
concepts.summary: People combining their skills to reach a shared goal.
concepts.definition: Teamwork is when people work together, share tasks and support each other to achieve something they could not do alone.
how: Agree on a clear shared goal.
Divide tasks according to strengths and set deadlines.
Communicate openly, listen and help each other.
concepts.why: Teams can solve bigger problems and produce better ideas than individuals alone.
concepts.example: A group project works well when each member researches one part and they combine their work.

concepts.title: Leadership
concepts.summary: Guiding and supporting others toward a shared goal.
concepts.definition: Leadership is the ability to influence and support a group to achieve a goal. Good leaders listen, take responsibility and serve others.
how: Set a clear direction and explain why it matters.
Listen to the team and use their strengths.
Take responsibility, stay fair and lead by example.
concepts.why: Good leadership helps groups stay focused and treat people with respect.
concepts.example: A class captain who listens to classmates and helps organise tasks shows leadership.

concepts.title: Communication
concepts.summary: Sharing information and ideas clearly and listening well.
concepts.definition: Communication is the exchange of information through speaking, writing, listening and body language. It works best when the message is clear and the listener understands.
how: Decide what you want to say and who you are saying it to.
Speak or write clearly and check understanding.
Listen actively and respond respectfully.
concepts.why: Clear communication prevents misunderstandings and builds strong relationships.
concepts.example: Explaining a task step by step and asking 'does that make sense?' improves understanding.

concepts.title: Fractions
concepts.summary: Numbers that show part of a whole.
concepts.definition: A fraction shows how many equal parts of a whole you have. The denominator (bottom) says how many parts the whole is divided into, and the numerator (top) says how many you have.
how: Split the whole into equal parts shown by the denominator.
Count the parts you have, shown by the numerator.
To add or subtract, use a common denominator.
concepts.why: Fractions are used in cooking, money, measurement and sharing.
concepts.example: If a pizza is cut into 4 equal slices and you eat 1, you have eaten 1/4 of the pizza.

concepts.title: Algebra
concepts.summary: Using letters to stand for unknown numbers and solving for them.
concepts.definition: Algebra uses symbols such as x to represent unknown numbers. An equation states that two expressions are equal, and solving it means finding the value that makes it true.
how: Identify the unknown and give it a letter.
Write an equation that describes the situation.
Do the same operation to both sides until the letter is alone.
concepts.why: Algebra helps solve problems where some information is missing.
concepts.example: If x + 3 = 10, subtract 3 from both sides to get x = 7.

concepts.title: Probability
concepts.summary: A measure of how likely an event is to happen.
concepts.definition: Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that describes how likely an event is. 0 means impossible and 1 means certain.
how: Count the number of possible equally likely outcomes.
Count how many of those outcomes are the event you want.
Divide the wanted outcomes by the total outcomes.
concepts.why: Probability helps us make decisions under uncertainty, from weather to games.
concepts.example: The probability of getting heads when flipping a fair coin is 1/2.

concepts.title: Evolution
concepts.summary: How species change over generations through natural selection.
concepts.definition: Evolution is the change in the inherited characteristics of populations over generations. Natural selection means individuals with helpful traits are more likely to survive and reproduce.
how: Individuals in a population vary in their traits.
Some traits help survival and reproduction more than others.
Those helpful traits become more common over many generations.
concepts.why: Evolution explains the diversity of life and how species adapt to their environments.
concepts.example: Bacteria that survive antibiotics pass on resistance, making future infections harder to treat.

concepts.title: DNA
concepts.summary: The molecule that carries the instructions for building and running living things.
concepts.definition: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a molecule shaped like a twisted ladder that stores genetic information. Genes are sections of DNA that carry instructions for traits.
how: DNA is made of four bases (A, T, C, G) arranged in a sequence.
The sequence spells out instructions for making proteins.
Genes are passed from parents to offspring, creating inherited traits.
concepts.why: DNA explains inheritance, health, and how living things grow and function.
concepts.example: Eye colour and blood type are influenced by genes inherited from your parents.

concepts.title: Plate tectonics
concepts.summary: The theory that Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that move.
concepts.definition: Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth's lithosphere is divided into large plates that slowly move over the mantle, causing earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building.
how: Heat from Earth's interior causes slow movement in the mantle.
The plates above move, colliding, separating or sliding past each other.
Their interactions create mountains, earthquakes, volcanoes and ocean trenches.
concepts.why: It explains the location of earthquakes, volcanoes and continents.
concepts.example: The Himalayas formed as two plates pushed together over millions of years.

analogies.text: Think of the internet like a road network: data is traffic, routers are junctions and servers are the destinations.
The brain is like a computer: neurons are circuits, memory is storage and thinking is processing.
A cell is like a factory: the nucleus is the office with instructions, mitochondria are the power station and the membrane is the gate.
An ecosystem is like a machine: every part has a job, and removing one part can make the whole thing stop working well.
An algorithm is like a recipe: follow the steps in order and you get the result.

heuristics.text: Look for the chain: what triggered it, what conditions allowed it, and what made it worse.
Trace the consequences: short-term and long-term, direct and indirect, and who is affected.
Compare on the same criteria: purpose, cost, risk, benefit and who benefits.
List options, criteria and trade-offs, then choose the option with the best balance for your values.
Define the key term, give an example and say why it matters.
Find the parts, how they connect, and what feedback loops keep the system stable or push it to change.
